questions.stem: For data set 2283, find the bug: switch(x){case 1: y=1; case 2: y=2; break;} what is wrong?

options.misconception: Missing break lets execution continue into the next case
Incorrectly assumed switch requires a non-integer selector
Confused an optional default with a required clause

options.text: The condition must be a range
options.misconception: Mistook switch matching for interval comparison

questions.explanation: Option A is the key because the first case has no break, so execution falls through into the second case and overwrites y Option B fails because switch selectors can be integer expressions in C Option C fails because the default label is optional, not required Option D fails because switch matches discrete case labels, not ranges.
questions.hint: Look for a case group that lacks a terminating break statement.

questions.stem: For data set 2284, find the bug: if (x = 5) { puts("yes"); } what is wrong?

options.misconception: A single equals sign stores a value instead of testing it
Misread a nonzero assignment as a false truth value
Confused a comparison bug with a declaration error
Mistook a logic error for a syntax error

questions.explanation: Option A is the key because the single equals sign assigns five to x and then tests that nonzero value as true, so the condition never compares Option B fails because a nonzero assignment is treated as true, not false Option C fails because x is declared elsewhere; this is a logic error Option D fails because the statement is syntactically complete; the fault is logical.
questions.hint: Comparisons use a doubled operator, not a single equals sign.

questions.stem: For data set 2287, a sensor lab averages the readings 3, 5, 7; what mean is printed?
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum of the readings divided by their count. Adding 3, 5, and 7 gives 15, and dividing by three yields 5. Remember that dividing by the number of readings, not by the largest one, produces the mean.
questions.hint: Add all readings and divide by how many there are.

questions.stem: For data set 2290, an array holds 11 elements; what is the index of its final element?
questions.explanation: C arrays are zero-indexed, so an array of 11 elements uses indices 0 through 10. The last index is one less than the element count, a classic off-by-one boundary that new programmers often miss.
questions.hint: Remember that indexing starts at zero, not one.

questions.stem: For data set 2291, a clinic records the remainder when 61 is divided by 5; what value is printed?
questions.explanation: The remainder operator gives what is left after dividing 61 by 5. Since 5 fits into 61 a whole number of times with 1 left over, the printed value is 1. Integer division alone would give the quotient instead.
questions.hint: Find the leftover after dividing evenly, not the quotient.

questions.explanation: The loop continues while i is strictly less than 9. Starting from 0, i takes the values 0 through 8, which is 9 distinct iterations. The strict less-than condition excludes 9 itself, so the count equals the bound.

questions.stem: For data set 2293, an engineer computes the C expression 15 << 2; what integer results?
questions.explanation: Shifting an integer left by two bit positions multiplies it by four. Therefore 15 << 2 equals 15 times 4, which is 60. A right shift would divide instead, and adding two would be a different operation entirely.
questions.hint: A left shift by n multiplies by two to the power of n.

questions.stem: For data set 2294, a program prints the integer quotient of 144 divided by 5; what appears?

questions.hint: Truncate the fractional part of the division result.
